item.title: Kawagoe (Little Edo): Storehouse Streets & Candy Alley — Guide
item.description: Kawagoe, nicknamed ‘Little Edo’ for its remarkably preserved streetscape, was a prosperous merchant town during the Edo period whose fireproof kurazukuri storehouses — thick-walled, black-tiled buildings — still line its main street today. A short walk away, Kashiya Yokocho (‘Candy Alley’) is a nostalgic lane of small shops selling traditional penny candies and rice crackers much as they did generations ago, making the combination one of the most complete slices of old Japan within easy reach of Tokyo.

item.title: Kawagoe Kimono Rental: Walk Little Edo in Period Costume — Guide
item.description: Kawagoe’s remarkably preserved Edo-period streetscape has made it one of the most popular destinations near Tokyo for kimono rental experiences, with dozens of shops offering a range of kimono and yukata styles, along with hair styling and accessories, for a half-day or full-day rental. Dressed visitors then wander the historic Kurazukuri storehouse street, Toki no Kane bell tower and Kashiya Yokocho candy alley, creating a genuinely photogenic sense of stepping back into old Japan.

item.title: Sawara Guide: Little Edo Canal Town, Grand Festival & Access
item.description: The merchant town of Sawara, in Katori, is the jewel of Chiba’s old townscapes — a beautifully preserved “Little Edo” where black-tiled merchant houses, willow trees and stone bridges line the Ono River canal. Once a prosperous river-trade hub, it retains a rare Edo-period atmosphere, best enjoyed on a leisurely boat ride down the canal or a stroll past its old sake breweries and the former home of Ino Tadataka, the surveyor who first mapped Japan accurately.

item.title: Kawagoe Little Edo: Complete Walking Guide
item.description: Thirty minutes north of Ikebukuro, the city of Kawagoe preserves one of the most intact merchant townscapes in the entire Kanto region. During the Edo period (1603–1868), Kawagoe served as a major provisioning center for the capital, and its prosperous merchants built their storehouses with an unusual solidity: thick walls of layered clay plaster on timber frames, designed to resist the fires that periodically devastated wooden Edo. When Edo burned, Kawagoe’s kura survived.
